items.title: AskLaw RAG — Turkish Criminal Law Assistant
items.body:
A Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) assistant that answers plain-language questions about the Turkish Criminal Code (TCK — Law No. 5237). Ask the way anyone would — _"my neighbor slapped me, what can I do?"_ — and get an answer grounded in the actual statute, with the exact articles it relied on.

**🔗 Live Demo:** [https://huggingface.co/spaces/borakosalay/Ask-Law-RAG](https://huggingface.co/spaces/borakosalay/Ask-Law-RAG)

## Why I Built This

Most people's first contact with the law happens the moment something goes wrong — someone insults them, breaks their stuff, threatens them — and the first question in their head is almost always the same: _"Is this even legal? Do I have a right here?"_ But the moment you try to answer that, you hit a wall: the law doesn't describe your problem in your words. You say _"someone hit me,"_ the law says _"intentional injury."_ There's often not a single shared word between the two.

That gap always felt unfair to me. To find out whether you even have a case, you first have to get past a translation layer — legal jargon — that most people were never taught. So I built a tool that lets anyone, with zero legal vocabulary, ask in their own words and find out whether the thing that happened to them (or just something they're curious about) actually has a place in the law.

![chat-with-ai](/images/uploads/demo.png)

## Features

- **Plain-language input** — ask in ordinary Turkish, no legal terms required.
- **Strictly source-grounded** — answers only from the retrieved article text, never invented.
- **Cites its sources** — every answer shows the exact articles it used (e.g. _TCK m.86 — Kasten yaralama_).
- **Refuses to guess** — if no relevant article is found, it says so instead of hallucinating.
- **Always disclaims** — appends a reminder that this is information, not legal advice.
- **Trivially updatable** — when the law changes, you just edit the knowledge base; no retraining.

## Tech Stack

| Layer | Choice |
| PDF extraction | pdfplumber + regex |
| Embeddings | sentence-transformers · BAAI/bge-m3 (local) |
| Vector store | faiss-cpu (IndexFlatIP, cosine) |
| Question generation | Groq LLM |
| Answer generation | Groq · llama-4-scout-17b-16e-instruct |
| Frontend | Streamlit |
| Hosting | Hugging Face Spaces (CPU Basic, free) |

## The Software

**Bridging the vocabulary gap.** This is the core of the whole thing. Citizens and statutes use completely different words for the same act — a user types _"birini dövdüm"_ ("I hit someone"), the law says _"kasten yaralama"_ ("intentional injury"), with zero lexical overlap, so searching the article texts directly just retrieves the wrong articles. So I flipped it: for each article I had an LLM generate dozens of realistic, everyday-language questions (_"my neighbor slapped me," "someone threatened to kill me"_), each tagged with its source article, and embedded those alongside the article texts. Now a colloquial query matches a similar generated question, which points straight to the right article.

**RAG, not fine-tuning — so it can't make things up.** For a legal tool, accuracy is non-negotiable, and fine-tuning a model to "memorize" the law invites hallucinated article numbers and penalties. RAG keeps the law in an external, searchable store and feeds only the relevant text to the model at answer time. A strict system prompt does the rest: use only the directly relevant articles, never invent anything, always cite the article (_"TCK m.86'ya göre..."_), and if the articles don't cover the question, say so instead of guessing. A low temperature (0.3) keeps answers faithful and consistent.

**A clean knowledge base.** The raw TCK PDF doesn't parse cleanly, so a dedicated pipeline (pdfplumber + regex) handles the mess — robust article detection across formatting variants, correct titles, no bleed between articles, and repealed (_mülga_) articles flagged. Output: 345 articles as JSONL with metadata.

**Deduplicated retrieval.** The index holds both article and question vectors, so a query pulls 20 candidates, then collapses them to the top 5 unique articles before generation.

***

⚠️ _This is an informational tool, not legal advice. Outputs can be incomplete or wrong and may not reflect the latest amendments — for any real legal matter, consult a licensed attorney._

items.title: Solid Rocket Propellant Performance Classification
items.body:
## Overview

[](https://github.com/boraiks/Rocket-Propellant-Analysis#-overview)

Solid rocket propellants remain a critical technology in both defense and space exploration, offering lower production costs and simpler manufacturing compared to liquid-fueled alternatives. However, the challenge lies in producing _high-quality_ propellant consistently.

This project applies machine learning classification techniques to a solid rocket propellant dataset to identify which chemical and physical parameters most strongly determine propellant performance quality. Three classifiers — **Random Forest**, **Support Vector Machine (SVM)**, and **K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN)** — are trained, evaluated, and compared.

***

## Dataset

[](https://github.com/boraiks/Rocket-Propellant-Analysis#-dataset)

- **Source:** [Kaggle — Solid Rocket Propellant Burning Rate Data](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/ranjeetsingh7/solid-rocket-propellant-data-burning-rate)
- **Observations:** 137 samples
- **Features:** 18 variables

### Feature Groups

[](https://github.com/boraiks/Rocket-Propellant-Analysis#feature-groups)

| Category | Features |
| --- | --- |
| High-energy oxidizers | NC+NG (Nitrocellulose + Nitroglycerin), RDX, HMX, CL-20 |
| Metal additives | nAl (nano), mAl (micro), Al (raw), nAlN, Al₂O₃, nNi |
| Plasticizers & stabilizers | DEP (Diethyl Phthalate), nDPN (n-Diphenylamine) |
| Combustion regulators | Catalyst, Burning rate inhibitor |
| Measurements | Pressure (MPa), Burning rate (mm/s) |

### Custom Target Variable

[](https://github.com/boraiks/Rocket-Propellant-Analysis#custom-target-variable)

A novel **Propulsion Quality** metric was derived to convert this regression dataset into a classification problem:

```plain
Propulsion Quality = Burning Rate / Pressure  →  min-max normalized to [0, 1]
```

This was then divided into three balanced classes using the 33rd and 67th percentiles:

| Class | Propulsion Quality | Count |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Low (0) | < 0.167 | 45 |
| Med (1) | 0.167 – 0.327 | 47 |
| High (2) | > 0.327 | 45 |

***

## Repository Structure

[](https://github.com/boraiks/Rocket-Propellant-Analysis#-repository-structure)

```plain
├── Rocket_Propellant_Analysis.ipynb        # Full analysis notebook
├── images/                                 # Plots and visualizations
│   ├── correlation_heatmap.png
│   ├── feature_histograms.png
│   ├── boxplots.png
│   ├── class_distribution.png
│   ├── confusion_matrices.png
│   ├── model_comparison.png
│   ├── lime_importance.png
│   └── venn_diagram.png
└── README.md
```

***

## 

## Methodology

[](https://github.com/boraiks/Rocket-Propellant-Analysis#%EF%B8%8F-methodology)

### 1. Data Preprocessing

[](https://github.com/boraiks/Rocket-Propellant-Analysis#1-data-preprocessing)

- Null value check (no missing values found)
- Label encoding: Low → 0, Med → 1, High → 2
- Propulsion Quality and Propulsion Class removed from feature inputs to prevent data leakage

### 2. Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)

[](https://github.com/boraiks/Rocket-Propellant-Analysis#2-exploratory-data-analysis-eda)

- Correlation heatmap
- Feature distribution histograms
- Per-class boxplots
- Class distribution bar chart

### 3. Train / Test Split & Scaling

[](https://github.com/boraiks/Rocket-Propellant-Analysis#3-train--test-split--scaling)

- 80% training / 20% test split (stratified)
- `StandardScaler` fitted **only on training data** to prevent data leakage

### 4. Models

[](https://github.com/boraiks/Rocket-Propellant-Analysis#4-models)

| Model | Key Parameters |
| --- | --- |
| Random Forest | `max_depth=5`, `min_samples_leaf=5`, `n_estimators=100` |
| SVM | Default `SVC` with `probability=True` |
| KNN | `k=7` (selected by cross-validating k=1..15; upper bound ≈ √137 ≈ 11.7) |

### 5. Evaluation Metrics

[](https://github.com/boraiks/Rocket-Propellant-Analysis#5-evaluation-metrics)

- Accuracy, F1-Score (macro), Recall/Sensitivity, Precision, G-Score

### 6. Interpretability

[](https://github.com/boraiks/Rocket-Propellant-Analysis#6-interpretability)

- **LIME** (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations) — chosen over SHAP for better performance on small datasets and non-tree models
- **Venn diagram** — visualizing feature overlap across models' top-5 important features

***

## Results

[](https://github.com/boraiks/Rocket-Propellant-Analysis#-results)

### Model Performance (Test Set)

[](https://github.com/boraiks/Rocket-Propellant-Analysis#model-performance-test-set)

| Model | Accuracy | F1-Score | Recall | G-Score |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Random Forest** | **0.643** | **0.639** | **0.652** | **0.487** |
| SVM | 0.571 | 0.561 | 0.581 | 0.385 |
| KNN (k=7) | 0.536 | 0.511 | 0.548 | 0.314 |

**Random Forest achieved the best test performance across all metrics.**

### Model Comparison

[](https://github.com/boraiks/Rocket-Propellant-Analysis#model-comparison)

![Model Comparison](https://github.com/boraiks/Rocket-Propellant-Analysis/raw/main/images/model_comparison.png)

### Confusion Matrices (Test Set)

[](https://github.com/boraiks/Rocket-Propellant-Analysis#confusion-matrices-test-set)

![Confusion Matrices](https://github.com/boraiks/Rocket-Propellant-Analysis/raw/main/images/confusion_matrices.png)

- **Low class (0)** was the easiest to classify correctly across all models
- **Med class (1)** caused the most misclassifications — likely due to its overlapping characteristics with Low and High

### Correlation Heatmap

[](https://github.com/boraiks/Rocket-Propellant-Analysis#correlation-heatmap)

![Correlation Heatmap](https://github.com/boraiks/Rocket-Propellant-Analysis/raw/main/images/correlation_heatmap.png)

Key correlations found:

- `Burning rate inhibitor` ↔ `Burning rate`: **−0.85** (strong negative)
- `Catalyst` ↔ `Burning rate`: **+0.60** (strong positive)
- `Burning rate` ↔ `Propulsion Class`: **+0.68** (target variable's strongest predictor)

### Feature Distributions

[](https://github.com/boraiks/Rocket-Propellant-Analysis#feature-distributions)

![Feature Histograms](https://github.com/boraiks/Rocket-Propellant-Analysis/raw/main/images/feature_histograms.png)

![Boxplots by Class](https://github.com/boraiks/Rocket-Propellant-Analysis/raw/main/images/boxplots.png)

***

## Feature Importance (LIME)

[](https://github.com/boraiks/Rocket-Propellant-Analysis#-feature-importance-lime)

![LIME Feature Importance](https://github.com/boraiks/Rocket-Propellant-Analysis/raw/main/images/lime_importance.png)

Top-5 features per model:

| Rank | Random Forest | SVM | KNN |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Pressure, MPa | nDPN, % | nDPN, % |
| 2 | Burning rate inhibitor | Pressure, MPa | Pressure, MPa |
| 3 | Burning rate, mm/sec | HMX, % | CL-20 |
| 4 | NC+NG, % | Al₂O₃, % | Burning rate inhibitor |
| 5 | others, % | mAl, % | Al |

### Feature Overlap Across Models

[](https://github.com/boraiks/Rocket-Propellant-Analysis#feature-overlap-across-models)

![Venn Diagram](https://github.com/boraiks/Rocket-Propellant-Analysis/raw/main/images/venn_diagram.png)

**Pressure (MPa)** is the only feature in the top-5 of all three models — confirming it as the single most decisive variable. This aligns with combustion science literature where operating pressure is a fundamental driver of solid propellant burning behavior.

***

## References

[](https://github.com/boraiks/Rocket-Propellant-Analysis#-references)

- [Kaggle Dataset — Solid Rocket Propellant Burning Rate](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/ranjeetsingh7/solid-rocket-propellant-data-burning-rate)
- [ML-based burning rate prediction (Wiley/Propellants Journal)](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/prep.202200267)
- [Effect of aluminum content on burning rate (ScienceDirect)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0016236113004456)

***

## License

[](https://github.com/boraiks/Rocket-Propellant-Analysis#-license)

The dataset is sourced from Kaggle under its respective license. All analysis code is available for educational use.

items.title: Thrust Vector Control Model Rocket
items.body:
A hobbyist model rocketry project I started purely out of my obsession with space tech. It explores custom flight mechanics and Thrust Vector Control — so I can figure out how rockets actually work, test things safely, and learn by doing

## **About TVC Mount**

[](https://github.com/boraiks/rocket1003#about-tvc-mount)

**For RocketV2, I completely redesigned the TVC mount. My first version used four high-torque servos, which ended up being way too heavy and bulky. I stripped it down to a new 3D-modeled mount using just two tiny 9g servos for the X and Y axes — so I can shave off dead weight and keep the rocket as light and efficient as possible. Check out the nearly completed design below.**

> UPDATE: I shifted to a more efficient design with 9g servos. Check out my nearly completed TVC design below.
> {{model}}

## **About Manual Controller**

[](https://github.com/boraiks/rocket1003#about-manual-controller)

**I coded a manual controller with C#, to test and control the servos with my joystick, making it easier to integrate the limits into the model.**

> I thought it might also be good to have the ability to control it manually in case of emergencies like airbrakes, drag chute for safe landing etc, so I might add more buttons and functions in the future.
> ![MANUALCONTROLLER](https://github.com/boraiks/rocket1003/raw/main/manualController/img/manualController.gif)[](https://github.com/boraiks/rocket1003/blob/main/manualController/img/manualController.gif)

## **About Flight Computer**

[](https://github.com/boraiks/rocket1003#about-flight-computer)

**As part of my TVC (Thrust Vector Control) RocketV2 project, I've designed a detailed flight computer schematic. It includes connections for an Arduino Nano, MPU6050, and BMP280 sensors. To create this schematic, I had to make some custom .lbr files for the Eagle program, as they aren't available online.**

> If you're interested in these files, you can find them in the `flightComputer` directory of this repository. Also check schematic (basic outline for now) down below.![ROCKETV2-PCB](https://github.com/boraiks/rocket1003/raw/main/flightComputer/img/PCB_OUTLINE4.png)

## **Tests**

[](https://github.com/boraiks/rocket1003#tests)

Gyro Test:

> ![FLIGHTCOMPUTERGYROTEST1](https://github.com/boraiks/rocket1003/raw/main/flightComputer/img/FlightComputerGyroTest.gif)[](https://github.com/boraiks/rocket1003/blob/main/flightComputer/img/FlightComputerGyroTest.gif)

## NOTICE

[](https://github.com/boraiks/rocket1003#notice)

As of September 25, 2024 I've stopped the project, feel free to follow up and ask questions but I will most likely not update anymore about TVC—at least for a while. It's been a great journey and thank you to everyone who supported me for the past year.

items.title: Book Buddy -  Handheld E-Ink Reader
items.body:
A pocket-sized, distraction-free reading device I built around an ESP32-C3 and a tiny E-ink screen. It stores books on board, accepts uploads over its own Wi-Fi hotspot, and runs entirely offline — so I can read anywhere without ever reaching for my phone.

***

## Why I Built This

I love reading, but I can't always carry a stack of physical books around with me. I also wanted something that works completely **independently from my phone** — no notifications, no apps, no temptation to switch to something else.

That separation turned out to matter more than I expected. This little device genuinely helped with my focus and rebuilt my reading habit. Now it's a tiny digital handbook I can slip into my pocket and pull out to read anywhere — on a bus, in a queue, wherever I happen to be.

![](/images/uploads/bookbuddyv2.gif)

***

## Features

- **100% Offline** — every book lives in on-board storage; no connection needed to read.
- **Wireless Uploads** — the device hosts its own Wi-Fi hotspot and web UI for sending books straight to storage.
- **Single-Button Navigation** — short / double / long press gestures drive the whole interface.
- **Resume Where You Left Off** — reading position is saved per-book and restored automatically.
- **Hardware Battery Gauge** — live battery percentage, calibrated to the ESP32-C3's ADC.
- **Power-Friendly** — E-ink, a master cut-off switch, and a screensaver keep battery drain minimal.
- **Anti-Ghosting Cover Mode** — a custom startup/idle image keeps the panel healthy.

***

## What's Inside

| Component | Part | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Microcontroller | ESP32-C3 SuperMini | Minimal clone |
| Display | 2.13" E-ink | GxEPD2 compatible · 212 × 104 px |
| Charging | TP4056 LiPo Charger Module | USB charging + protection |
| Battery | 3.7V LiPo |  |
| Battery Sensing | 2 × 10 kΩ Resistors | Voltage divider |
| Input | 1 × Push Button | Single-button control |
| Power | ON/OFF Toggle Switch | Master cut-off |

***

## The Software

- **Hybrid Font System** — hardware bitmap fonts render sharp, crisp UI elements, while a vector font (`FreeSans9pt7b`) gives smooth, book-like body text while reading.
- **Smart Pagination** — page limits are computed dynamically from absolute character counts, saved to `.pos` files so resume is seamless and accurate.
- **Local Web Server (Hotspot)** — the device emits a Wi-Fi access point named \*\*`E-Reader`\*\*. Connect to it and open the web UI to format, parse, and upload PDFs directly into storage as raw text.
- **Screensaver / Cover Mode** — a custom 1-bit BMP (generated with Image2CPP) shows on startup and after 60 seconds of menu inactivity, saving power and preventing screen ghosting.
- **Hardware Battery Monitor** — real-time battery percentage in the bottom-right corner, calibrated specifically to the ESP32-C3's internal ADC millivolt reference.

***

## Single-Button Controls

The entire interface is driven by one push button, using three press gestures:

| Gesture | Action |
| --- | --- |
| **Short Press** | Move cursor / Next page |
| **Double Press** | Previous page / Back to menu |
| **Long Press** (> 500 ms) | Select / Enter menu / Save & exit book |

***

## How It Works

### Books live on the device

Once a book is on board, everything happens locally — there's no internet involved in reading. Books are stored in the ESP32-C3's LittleFS flash, and the firmware keeps track of your exact character position in a `.pos` file, so you always resume precisely where you stopped.

### Converting PDFs without overwhelming the chip

This was the most interesting problem to solve. The ESP32-C3 has very little memory and processing power — nowhere near enough to run a Wi-Fi hotspot **and** convert a multi-megabyte PDF into text at the same time. Doing both at once simply isn't possible on a chip this small.

So instead of asking the microcontroller to do the heavy lifting, I push the work to whatever device you're uploading from. When you connect to the hotspot and pick a PDF, the conversion runs in **JavaScript, right in your browser** — using the power of your phone or laptop rather than the ESP32.

Better still, it happens **progressively, in chunks**. The PDF is converted piece by piece, and each piece is streamed to the device as it becomes ready — for example, once roughly 10% is converted, that 10% is uploaded, then the next chunk follows. This keeps the ESP32's memory footprint tiny no matter how large the original file is, because the chip only ever has to handle small, manageable bits of plain text.

***

## What I Learned

This project taught me a lot of hands-on electronics and embedded software:

- **Reading a battery through a GPIO pin.** Using a simple two-resistor voltage divider, I learned how to safely scale the LiPo's voltage down into a range the ADC can read — and turn that reading into a reliable battery percentage.
- **Saving space with LittleFS.** I was genuinely surprised how much storage I could reclaim with LittleFS; it's what makes fitting real books onto such a tiny chip practical in the first place.
- **Offloading heavy work to the client.** The biggest lesson: when the hardware can't do something, move the work somewhere that can. Converting PDFs in the browser and streaming them in chunks was the key that made the whole project possible on a chip with this little memory.

***

## The 3D-Printed Case

Every reader needs a home, so I designed a custom 3D-printed case for it. You can browse the 3D model here:

{{model}}

items.title: Playwright Pytest Demo
items.body:
UI and API test automation for a small industrial monitoring web app, built with **Playwright** and **pytest**. The application under test is intentionally minimal — the focus of this project is the **test suite and the engineering practices around it**, not the app itself.

## What this project demonstrates

[](https://github.com/boraiks/playwright-pytest-demo#what-this-project-demonstrates)

- **UI and API testing in one suite** — browser-driven tests through Playwright, plus direct API tests against the same service.
- **Positive, negative, and boundary testing** — valid flows, rejected bad input, and edge cases: HTTP 401 for bad credentials, 404 for unknown resources, and 422 for out-of-range values.
- **Test infrastructure** — a pytest fixture automatically starts the system under test before the tests run and shuts it down afterward, so `pytest` is the only command needed.
- **Continuous integration** — every push runs the full suite on a clean machine via GitHub Actions.
- **AI-assisted test authoring** — tests generated and verified with GitHub Copilot and the Playwright MCP server, which lets the agent inspect the real DOM and write tests against it instead of guessing selectors.

## Tech stack

[](https://github.com/boraiks/playwright-pytest-demo#tech-stack)

| Layer | Choice |
| --- | --- |
| System under test | FastAPI + a small static HTML/JS UI |
| UI testing | Playwright (`page` fixture, `data-testid` locators) |
| API testing | Playwright (`APIRequestContext`) |
| Test runner | pytest + `pytest-playwright` |
| Test infrastructure | pytest fixture that auto-starts / stops the app |
| CI | GitHub Actions (runs on every push) |
| AI-assisted authoring | Playwright MCP + GitHub Copilot (agent mode) |

[](https://github.com/boraiks/playwright-pytest-demo#how-it-works)

## Getting started

[](https://github.com/boraiks/playwright-pytest-demo#getting-started)

```plain
# install dependencies
pip install -r requirements.txt

# install the browser Playwright drives
playwright install chromium

# run the whole suite (the app starts and stops automatically)
python -m pytest
```

Demo login: **operator / siemens123**

## Project structure

[](https://github.com/boraiks/playwright-pytest-demo#project-structure)

```plain
app/                  # system under test (FastAPI + a small static UI)
  main.py             # REST API endpoints + serves the login page
  static/index.html   # login page / dashboard
tests/                # the test suite: UI, API, and an AI-generated test
conftest.py           # fixtures: auto-starts and stops the app under test
requirements.txt      # dependencies
.github/workflows/    # CI pipeline (runs pytest on every push)
.vscode/mcp.json      # Playwright MCP server config for AI-assisted testing

```

## The system under test

[](https://github.com/boraiks/playwright-pytest-demo#the-system-under-test)

A small FastAPI app that serves a login page and a REST API for industrial devices — listing devices, reading sensor values, and updating an alarm threshold with input validation. It exists only to give the tests a realistic target and is deliberately kept small.

## AI-assisted testing

[](https://github.com/boraiks/playwright-pytest-demo#ai-assisted-testing)

Part of the suite was authored using the [Playwright MCP](https://github.com/microsoft/playwright-mcp) server together with GitHub Copilot in agent mode. The agent opens a real browser, inspects the live page, and writes a Playwright test based on what it actually sees. Every AI-generated test was reviewed and verified by hand before being kept.

items.title: Saucedemo QA
items.body:
Manual and automated QA of [SauceDemo](https://www.saucedemo.com/), a demo e-commerce application. This project shows the full path from **exploratory testing** to a written **bug report** to an **automated regression test** built from that report.

## What this project demonstrates

[](https://github.com/boraiks/saucedemo-qa#what-this-project-demonstrates)

- **Exploratory testing** of the main purchase flow (login, inventory, cart, checkout), using a reference account to establish correct behavior.
- **Professional bug reports** — documented defects with reproduction steps, expected vs. actual results, and severity ratings (see [`bug-reports.md`](https://github.com/boraiks/saucedemo-qa/blob/main/bug-reports.md)).
- **Bug triage discipline** — suspected issues were validated against a known-good reference account before being reported, and false positives were ruled out instead of filed.
- **Automated regression testing** — a Playwright test that encodes correct behavior; it passes against the working account and catches a real defect when run against the broken one.

## Approach

[](https://github.com/boraiks/saucedemo-qa#approach)

Two SauceDemo accounts were used deliberately: `standard_user` as a **baseline** expected to work correctly, and `problem_user` as the account **under test**. Comparing the two made it possible to tell genuine defects apart from expected behavior — and to discard false alarms instead of filing incorrect reports.

[](https://github.com/boraiks/saucedemo-qa#how-it-works)

## From bug report to regression test

[](https://github.com/boraiks/saucedemo-qa#from-bug-report-to-regression-test)

The automated test was built directly from one of the defects found during exploratory testing — the broken sort functionality. Here is the report it is based on:

***

**Defect — Inventory: sort dropdown options are unresponsive**

_Environment:_ saucedemo.com · user: `problem_user` · Chrome

_Steps to reproduce:_

1. Log in as `problem_user` / `secret_sauce`.
2. Click the sort dropdown menu at the top right to open it.
3. Attempt to select a different sorting option (e.g., "Price (high to low)").

_Expected result:_ The selected option is applied and the products are reordered based on the new criteria.

_Actual result:_ The dropdown opens, but clicking a sorting option triggers no action. The selection is ignored and the product order does not change.

_Severity:_ Medium — restricts navigation and user experience, though it does not outright block the purchasing path.

***

From this finding, `tests/test_sorting.py` was written to encode the _correct_ behavior: after selecting "Price (low to high)", the product prices must be in ascending order. The test passes for `standard_user` (where sorting works) and fails for `problem_user` (where it is broken) — turning a manual observation into an automated check that catches the defect on every run.

## Tech stack

[](https://github.com/boraiks/saucedemo-qa#tech-stack)

Playwright · pytest · pytest-playwright · GitHub Actions

## Getting started

[](https://github.com/boraiks/saucedemo-qa#getting-started)

```plain
pip install -r requirements.txt
playwright install chromium
python -m pytest
```

## Project structure

[](https://github.com/boraiks/saucedemo-qa#project-structure)

```plain
tests/test_sorting.py   # automated regression test (Playwright + pytest)
docs/bug-reports.md     # test plan + documented defects
requirements.txt        # dependencies
.github/workflows/      # CI (runs the tests on every push)
```

## Notes

[](https://github.com/boraiks/saucedemo-qa#notes)

The automated tests run against the **live** SauceDemo site, so they depend on that site being reachable and unchanged. A failure can therefore reflect an external issue (site downtime or a change on Sauce Labs' side) rather than a problem in this repository — a trade-off worth keeping in mind for tests that target a third-party application.

items.title: Mail-Agent — AI Email Categorizer
items.body:
An autonomous assistant that reads your incoming job application emails, figures out the outcome (offer, rejection, or automated notification), and neatly labels them in your Gmail. 

***

## Why I Built This

Managing job applications generates a high volume of inbox noise. Every incoming email requires manual triage just to figure out if it's an interview invite, a standard rejection, or an automated portal message.

I quickly realized that standard email filters don't work for this. Human Resources emails are notoriously polite. A rejection often starts with "**_We were highly impressed by your background..._**" which fools basic keyword filters into thinking it's good news.

I wanted a buffer—a personal assistant that opens the envelope first, reads between the lines, and tells me exactly what it is before I even start reading. So, I built an AI agent that runs in the background, categorizes the outcome, and organizes my inbox automatically.

***

## Features

- **Context-aware analysis** — understands the actual meaning of the email, not just keywords.
- **Smart categorization** — sorts emails into exactly 4 buckets: _Acceptance, Rejection, Sponsor (automated/portal emails),_ or _Other_.
- **Seamless Gmail integration** — applies native colored labels directly to your inbox.
- **Privacy-focused** — only requests permission to read and modify labels; it cannot delete your emails.

***

## Tech Stack

| Layer | Choice |
| --- | --- |
| Core Logic | Python |
| Email Access | Google Cloud / Gmail API (OAuth 2.0) |
| Intelligence | OpenAI · gpt-4o-mini |
| Action | Native Gmail Labels |

***

## The Software

**Understanding nuance, not just keywords.** This is the core problem the agent solves. A major edge case in job hunting is the "portal activation" email. Companies often send an automated _"Welcome to our career portal!"_ right after you apply. A basic script sees words like "Welcome" or "Successful" and flags it as good news. I explicitly engineered the AI prompt to recognize these structural nuances—forcing it to classify administrative/setup emails strictly as _Sponsor_ rather than _Acceptance_, eliminating false hope.

**A clean, disconnected pipeline.** The architecture is intentionally divided into single-responsibility modules. One script handles the secure OAuth handshake (`auth.py`), another safely extracts the sender and text from the latest email (`read.py`), and the final agent (`classify.py`) acts as the brain—sending the text to the LLM, deciding the category, and pushing the final label back to the Gmail servers. 

**Zero-friction workflow.** The agent doesn't require a separate dashboard or app. It does its thinking in the background and reflects its decisions directly in the Gmail UI you already use every day. You just open your inbox and immediately see a green _AI/Acceptance_ or a red _AI/Rejection_ tag waiting for you.

items.title: Exploded View — A Fusion 360 Add-In
items.body:
## Why I Built This

Making an exploded view by hand is tedious. You select a part, drag it, eyeball the spacing, select the next one, drag it, realise the first one is now in the way, start over. For an assembly with a dozen parts it's twenty minutes of fiddling — and if you change the model, you do it all again.

There are quick scripts out there that "explode" an assembly, but almost all of them do the same thing: move every part the same distance. The assembly separates from itself, sure — but the parts stay stacked on top of one another. You end up with a model that's floating in space and still unreadable.

I wanted the version that actually works: parts should separate **from each other**, not just from the block. The spacing should tell you the assembly order.

![before](/images/uploads/before.png)

![after](/images/uploads/after.png)

## Features

- **One button, one number** — click the toolbar button, type a gap distance, done.
- **Stepped separation** — the first layer moves one gap, the second moves two, the third moves three. Parts fan out in order instead of moving as a clump.
- **Layer awareness** — parts sitting at the same height (four bolts on the same face, for example) are treated as one layer and move together. They never get fanned out into a staircase.
- **Direction awareness** — parts above the reference move up, parts below move down.
- **Nothing hardcoded** — the gap is asked for at run time, so the same add-in works for a wristwatch and for a chassis.
- **Lives in the toolbar** — its own tab, next to SOLID and SURFACE, where you'd expect a Fusion tool to be.

## How It Works

### Figuring out where a part actually is

This turned out to be the first real problem. Fusion will happily tell you a component's transform — but that's the position of the part's _local origin_, and the origin is wherever the person modelling it happened to put it. It might be at the centre of a bolt, or at its tip, or floating fifty millimetres away in empty space because that's where the sketch started.

![](/images/uploads/stepped-vs-fixed.svg)

That's useless for asking "is this part above or below the base?" — a physical question that needs a physical answer. So instead I measure from the **centre of each part's bounding box**, which is computed from the actual geometry. It doesn't care where the origin was parked.

![](/images/uploads/layering.svg)

### Working out the layers

Once every part has a distance from the reference, they get sorted by that distance. The closest one becomes layer 1, the next distinct height becomes layer 2, and so on. The move distance is simply:

```plain
distance = layer number × gap
```

So the further up the stack a part sits, the further it travels — and gaps open up between every layer, not just between the parts and the base.

| Layer | Moves |
| 1 | 1 × gap |
| 2 | 2 × gap |
| 3 | 3 × gap |

The catch: what does "the same height" mean?

Two bolts sitting on the same face don't come back with identical numbers. You get `4.500` and `4.502`, because geometry never lines up perfectly. Compare them for equality and they land in different layers — and your four identical bolts fan out into a staircase.

So parts within a small tolerance of each other are grouped into one layer. It's a small detail, and it's the difference between an exploded view and a mess.

items.title: Modular Folding Wing EDF Observer UAV
items.body:
This project is an experimental **modular folding-wing observation UAV** developed around a specific constraint: the aircraft was designed to be carried inside a rocket and deployed after launch.

The aircraft therefore had to satisfy two very different requirements. During transport and deployment, it needed to be compact, mechanically protected, lightweight, and practical to manufacture. After deployment, it needed to become a functional fixed-wing aircraft with a stable aerodynamic configuration, a dedicated EDF propulsion system, and enough serviceability for repeated prototyping and testing.

The final concept is therefore not simply a small EDF aircraft. It is a **deployable aircraft system**, where packaging, deployment, aerodynamics, propulsion, structural design, and manufacturing constraints were considered together.

The current design target is approximately **600–620 g flight mass**.

![](/images/uploads/manuel3-v11.png)

![](/images/uploads/manuel3-v112.png)

## About the Airframe

The airframe is a lightweight fixed-wing platform with a rear-mounted electric ducted fan. The structure combines FDM-printed components, carbon-fiber reinforcement, mechanical fasteners, and heat-set inserts.

The design philosophy was to avoid making the aircraft unnecessarily heavy simply by increasing the amount of printed plastic. Material was instead concentrated around the areas that carry loads or experience repeated mechanical stress.

The wing uses carbon-fiber reinforcement for the main bending loads, while the printed structure provides the aerodynamic shape, interfaces, and load-transfer geometry.

![](/images/uploads/uav-exp.png)

## Airframe Architecture

The aircraft is divided into cooperating subsystems rather than being treated as one large printed body:

```plain
                 MAIN WING
                     │
              ┌──────┴──────┐
              │   FUSELAGE  │
              └──────┬──────┘
                     │
              AFT PROPULSION
                     │
              ┌──────┴──────┐
              │ MOTOR BLOCK │
              │    + EDF    │
              └─────────────┘
```

This separation was intentional. A prototype aircraft changes frequently during development: a motor mount may need to change, an EDF may need a different geometry, a damaged stator may need replacement, or the rear stabilization system may need modification.

The modular architecture allows individual subsystems to be replaced without rebuilding the entire aircraft.

## About the Folding Wings

![](/images/uploads/uav-fold.png)

## About the Wing

The main wing was developed around a low-Reynolds-number aerodynamic approach rather than using a generic flat plate.

The current wing is based on the **SD7037 airfoil**, selected as a suitable starting point for a lightweight aircraft operating at relatively low Reynolds numbers.

The established wing baseline is approximately:

| Parameter | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Span | 700 mm |
| Root chord | 90 mm |
| Tip chord | 64 mm |
| Airfoil | SD7037-based |
| Dihedral | \~5° |
| Root incidence | \~2° |
| Washout | \~2° |

The wing was designed for predictable low-speed behavior while remaining practical to manufacture.

![](/images/uploads/uav-wing.png)

## About the EDF Propulsion

The propulsion system is one of the most extensively optimized parts of the aircraft. The current system is based around an **EMAX RS2205 2300KV motor on 4S**.

The EDF was redesigned around the selected motor rather than simply placing an off-the-shelf fan inside the fuselage. The motor, rotor, duct, stator, wiring, and structural interfaces were treated as one system.

#### EDF Main Parameters

| Parameter | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Motor | EMAX RS2205 2300KV |
| Battery | 4S |
| Rotor diameter | Ø53.4 mm |
| Duct inner diameter | Ø55.2 mm |
| Rotor blades | 8 |
| Design RPM | \~31,600 RPM |
| Design axial velocity | \~25 m/s |
| Estimated thrust | \~248 gf |
| Estimated shaft power | \~73.5 W |
| Estimated torque | \~0.0222 N·m |
| Tip Mach number | \~0.27 |

These values are **design estimates**, not laboratory measurements. Actual performance depends on the manufactured rotor, motor, battery, ESC, inlet losses, temperature, clearances, and other real-world effects.

![](/images/uploads/uav-motor.png)

#### Rotor Design

The rotor uses **8 blades**, approximately **Ø53.4 mm** diameter, with an approximately **Ø29.5 mm** hub.

The blade was treated as a variable-geometry rotor rather than a constant-pitch propeller. Chord and blade angle change along the radius because the local flow conditions change from hub to tip.

The approximate radial design stations were:

| Radius | Chord | Local angle |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 13.0 mm | 12.4 mm | 5.5° |
| 14.9 mm | 12.2 mm | 5.5° |
| 17.5 mm | 12.3 mm | 5.5° |
| 20.0 mm | 11.7 mm | 5.0° |
| 22.5 mm | 10.5 mm | 4.8° |
| 24.8 mm | 9.0 mm | 4.3° |
| 26.7 mm | 7.6 mm | 3.8° |

![](/images/uploads/uav-prop.png)

#### Rotor Tip Clearance

The rotor operates inside a **Ø55.2 mm duct** with approximately **0.90 mm cold radial tip clearance**.

The clearance was selected with manufacturing tolerance, rotor runout, thermal expansion, and centrifugal effects in mind. Under the design assumptions, the estimated remaining clearance after these effects was approximately **0.32 mm**.

The objective was to find a practical compromise: small enough to limit tip leakage, but large enough to avoid rotor-to-duct contact.

![](/images/uploads/uav-motorblock.png)

#### EDF Inlet and Flow Path

The inlet uses approximately four capsule-shaped openings, each around **48 × 12 mm**. The effective inlet area was designed to be approximately **1.12 times the fan swept area**.

The intention is to reduce unnecessary inlet restriction without making the intake excessively large.

#### Nozzle and Tailcone

The downstream flow path was designed as a continuous system rather than stopping immediately after the rotor.

The nozzle exit is approximately **Ø45.6 mm**, with an approximate nozzle half-angle of **8°**. The tailcone uses an approximately **20.7° half-angle**.

## About the OGV / Stator

The EDF uses **5 Outlet Guide Vanes (OGVs)**. Their purpose is to recover part of the rotational energy left in the flow after the rotor and redirect the flow toward a more axial direction.

The OGVs are therefore not simple straight support struts. They use radially varying geometry and twist so that the flow turning changes through the span.

The nominal design intent was approximately **42° swirl reduction toward near-axial flow** while maintaining acceptable diffusion loading.

#### Why 5 OGVs?

The number of vanes was selected through an aerodynamic and structural trade-off.

An earlier 4-OGV configuration produced an estimated diffusion factor of approximately **DF ≈ 0.647**. This was considered too aggressive for the target design.

A 5-OGV configuration reduced the estimated diffusion factor to approximately **DF ≈ 0.578**.

The additional vane was therefore not added simply to make the structure stronger. It was a compromise between flow turning, diffusion, vane loading, structural stiffness, printability, and available space around the motor.

The final OGV axial chord is approximately **28 mm**.

#### OGV Structural Reinforcement

The first stator versions exposed an important FDM problem: long, relatively thin OGVs can be structurally weak and can vibrate under the periodic aerodynamic loading produced by a high-RPM rotor.

Individual support columns were considered, but these introduced undesirable local structures into the flow path.

The final design instead uses a **continuous 360° outer shroud** that captures approximately **60% of the OGV chord**.

This creates a continuous circumferential structural load path and provides a stiffer, more printable stator while avoiding large local obstructions in the flow.

The shroud also acts as the mechanical interface between the removable motor block and the surrounding propulsion shell.

## About the Rear Fins

The rear propulsion block uses **four fixed aerodynamic fins**. Their angular phase is approximately **22.5°** relative to the main body axes.

The orientation was selected from both aerodynamic and mechanical packaging requirements. The fins had to coexist with radial service screws, motor-block mounting geometry, the wiring route, and the surrounding fuselage/carrier.

Four equally distributed fins provide a simple and approximately symmetric arrangement. They are primarily intended to provide **passive pitch/yaw damping and directional stabilization**, rather than functioning as a large conventional tailplane.

The propulsion assembly remains within approximately the **Ø80 mm carrier envelope**, with a final outer diameter around **Ø78.46 mm**.

![](/images/uploads/uav-rearwings.png)

#### Why the Fins Are Not Simply Aligned With the Body

A simple arrangement would place the four fins directly on the horizontal and vertical axes. That configuration created conflicts with the mechanical service geometry.

The propulsion module already contains radial mounting points, fastener access, and a dedicated wiring route. Rotating the fin arrangement by approximately **22.5°** allows the aerodynamic surfaces and service hardware to coexist more efficiently.

This is representative of the general design philosophy: aerodynamic geometry and mechanical geometry cannot always be optimized independently.

## Optimization That I Made

The project went through several iterations before reaching the current configuration.

The major optimization areas were:

- motor selection,
- motor mounting geometry,
- EDF rotor diameter,
- duct diameter,
- rotor clearance,
- blade count,
- blade geometry,
- OGV count,
- OGV geometry,
- OGV structural reinforcement,
- inlet area,
- nozzle geometry,
- rear fin orientation,
- propulsion-module modularity,
- FDM manufacturing constraints.

#### Motor Mount Optimization

The motor mount was redesigned specifically for the **RS2205**. The actual motor mounting pattern was used instead of assuming a conventional rectangular bolt pattern or a single circular pitch diameter.

The mount also provides a central motor pilot, M3 clearance holes, controlled motor axial positioning, structural reinforcement around the fasteners, and a dedicated wire exit.

The motor wiring is routed toward the lower part of the assembly and kept outside the main rotor sweep.

#### Propulsion Modularity

The final architecture has several mechanical service levels.

#### Level 1 — Fuselage to propulsion shell

The aft propulsion shell can be separated from the main fuselage through a mechanical twist-lock interface.

#### Level 2 — Propulsion shell to motor block

The motor block is independently removable and retained using **four radial M3 fasteners** that engage heat-set inserts in the motor block.

#### Level 3 — Motor and rotor

The actual motor and rotor remain independently removable from the motor block.

This means that a motor failure or propulsion revision does not require replacing the entire rear fuselage.

![](/images/uploads/uav-motor.png)

## About Printing and Serviceability

The aircraft was designed specifically for FDM manufacturing rather than treating printing as an afterthought.

The design considers:

- layer orientation,
- wall thickness,
- screw clearances,
- heat-set insert installation,
- overhangs,
- rotor clearance,
- structural load paths,
- assembly tolerances,
- part replacement.

The objective is not simply to make a printable model. It is to make a **functional printed aircraft**.

#### Why Modular Printing?

A large aircraft component can take many hours to print. During prototyping, this becomes a serious problem if every small design change requires reprinting the entire aircraft.

The modular approach reduces this cost. A motor mount, stator, fin configuration, or EDF geometry can be redesigned and reprinted independently.

#### Heat-Set Inserts and Repeated Assembly

Heat-set inserts are used where screws may be removed repeatedly, particularly around the motor block and service interfaces.

The latest motor-block design uses approximately **Ø4.6 mm compact external head recesses** with approximately **Ø3.2 mm M3 shank clearance**. Final screw hardware should always be checked against the chosen fastener dimensions.

![](/images/uploads/uav-fasterners.png)

#### Structural Philosophy

The aircraft uses a hybrid structural approach.

**Printed components** provide aerodynamic surfaces, fuselage geometry, EDF ducting, stator structures, and mechanical interfaces.

**Carbon-fiber components** provide high stiffness where it matters most, especially in the main wing structure.

This division keeps the aircraft lighter than a fully solid printed structure while concentrating reinforcement along the main load paths.

## Mission Concept: Rocket-Deployed Observation UAV

The aircraft was designed as an **observation UAV**, not simply as a conventional RC aircraft.

The original concept was to place the aircraft inside a rocket or launch vehicle and deploy it after the rocket phase. This introduced a different design problem: the aircraft must first behave as a compact payload and then become a functional aircraft.

That requirement influenced the folding mechanism, compact fuselage, mechanical retention, lightweight construction, propulsion packaging, and serviceability.

#### From Rocket Payload to Observation Aircraft

The mission concept can be represented as:

```plain
         ROCKET PHASE
              │
              ▼
       Compact UAV payload
              │
              ▼
          Deployment
              │
              ▼
       Wing deployment
              │
              ▼
        Aircraft flight
              │
              ▼
      Observation / sensing
```

#### Development Philosophy

The project was developed iteratively through CAD, aerodynamic calculations, mechanical review, physical prototypes, and revision.

```plain
Requirement
    ↓
CAD concept
    ↓
Aerodynamic calculation
    ↓
Mechanical review
    ↓
FDM prototype
    ↓
Physical inspection / testing
    ↓
Revision
```

A major objective was to avoid changing too many variables at the same time. The EDF was therefore treated as its own subsystem so that the motor, rotor, duct, stator, wiring, and mounting could be developed and inspected as a system before final integration.

## Current Design Target

| System | Current target |
| --- | --- |
| Aircraft mass | \~600–620 g |
| Motor | EMAX RS2205 2300KV |
| Battery | 4S |
| EDF rotor | Ø53.4 mm / 8 blades |
| EDF duct | Ø55.2 mm |
| OGV | 5 vanes / \~28 mm chord |
| Rear fins | 4 / 22.5° phase |
| Wing span | 700 mm |
| Wing airfoil | SD7037-based |
| Primary wing reinforcement | Carbon fiber |
| Manufacturing | FDM + carbon fiber |

## Project Status

The aircraft has reached a functional physical-prototype stage, but the design remains experimental and can continue to evolve through flight and ground testing.

Future validation can include:

- measured EDF thrust,
- electrical power consumption,
- rotor balance and vibration,
- flight stability,
- CG and static-margin refinement,
- structural loads,
- deployment reliability,
- aerodynamic performance.

Calculated aerodynamic values in this documentation should therefore be treated as **design estimates rather than certified or experimentally validated performance specifications**.

## Safety and Experimental Use

This is an experimental aircraft design and is not a certified aircraft.

High-RPM EDF rotors can cause serious injury if they fail or are contacted during operation. Testing should be performed in an appropriate environment with suitable precautions.

The designer assumes no responsibility for damage, injury, misuse, or modifications made by other users.

## License and Terms of Use

This project is intended to be shared for **personal, educational, research, and non-commercial use**, subject to the project's current license terms.

Users may study the design, print the parts, modify the CAD, experiment with the aircraft, and create personal derivatives, provided that the applicable license terms are followed and the original designer is appropriately credited.

Suggested attribution:

> Original design by Bora Koşalay, 2026
> Project: Modular Folding-Wing EDF Observer UAV
> Original source: [https://borakosalay.me/project?p=modular-folding-wing-edf-observer-uav](https://borakosalay.me/project?p=modular-folding-wing-edf-observer-uav)

Commercial manufacturing, commercial redistribution, or selling the original design or derivatives should only be done if explicitly permitted by the final license published with the project.

**Important:** This section describes the project's intended terms. The actual legal permissions are defined by the license distributed with the project and should take precedence over this README.

## Credits

**Original design:** Bora Koşalay
**Project:** Modular Folding-Wing EDF Observer UAV
**Development:** CAD, aerodynamic design, propulsion design, mechanical design, FDM prototyping, and system integration

Official project page:

[https://borakosalay.me/project?p=modular-folding-wing-edf-observer-uav](https://borakosalay.me/project?p=modular-folding-wing-edf-observer-uav)

## Final Notes

The central idea behind this project was to combine several engineering constraints into one practical prototype:

> **How can a compact aircraft be designed to travel as a rocket payload, deploy into a functional fixed-wing UAV, and still remain practical to prototype, repair, and modify?**

The resulting aircraft is a combination of aerodynamic design, mechanical engineering, additive manufacturing, propulsion design, and deployment-oriented packaging.

The most important part of the project is therefore not a single component. It is the integration of all of these systems into one modular aircraft.
